entry.title: Quantumania 25 - Irritating Conveyor Belts
entry.content:
What we’re going to do with our solid United Nations-slash-Flerfer map is use it to represent both operations-on-things and things-being-operated-on. To do this, we’ll stick strictly to unit quaternions, which have modulus MATHI31 and are a closed set under multiplication: if you multiply two unit quaternions, the result is a unit quaternion. The things-being-operated-on are points in space, and the operations-on-things are rotations, and they are both simply points in our solid ball map. In fact, they are the only kind of quaternions in our map.

The unit quaternions describe all the possible pure rotations (with no scaling) that can be performed on a 3D space, just as unit complex numbers describe all pure rotations (with no scaling) on the complex plane. I can think of two possible nagging objections you might feel about this.

First, why does it need to have MATHI34 parameters if it’s a rotation in 3D space? Well, it sort of doesn’t: the constraint where their squares must sum to MATHI31 means that if you know three of them, the fourth is tied down to no more than two possible values, positive or negative:

\[w = \pm \sqrt{1 - (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)}\]

The role of the MATHI77 coordinate being thus diminished, our map almost insults it, giving the three spatial directions of the map space to the other three coordinates.

This is also important because it means that points in the northern (positive MATHI77) and southern (negative MATHI77) hemispheres of the unit quaternion 3-sphere are paired up. Once you pick values for MATHI28782c20792c207a29, there are only two points on the unit quaternion 3-sphere that you could be talking about. Or to refer to our ball-map, there’s a matching pair of points in the inner core and the outer shell.

Second, surely we only need two parameters to specify a point on a 2-sphere? Yes, but we also need to say how much to rotate by (and which of two ways, clockwise or anticlockwise). This works very much like complex rotation. The complex value MATHI31202b203069203d2031 is the identity operation, having no effect at all. The value MATHI30202b203169203d2069 rotates MATHI39305e5c63697263, and MATHI2d31202b203069 rotates MATHI3138305e5c63697263. In general, a pure rotation MATHI63 by angle MATHI5c7468657461 is given by:

\[c = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta\]

(Often an arbitrary complex number is labelled MATHI7a but I’ve switched to MATHI63 as we’ve been using MATHI7a for one of the ordinary spatial coordinates.)

So as MATHI5c7468657461 increases from MATHI30, the real part gradually falls as the imaginary part rises, and the two parts, interpreted as coordinates in a plane, describe a circular path. Such a complex number can be multiplied with any other complex number to move it around the origin by the angle MATHI5c7468657461, so we can think of it applying as an operator to all complex numbers, i.e. it rotates the entire plane.

So now we need to figure out the same thing for the quaternion space: what is the action of a unit quaternion on all the points in that space? So that we can see the results on our solid model, which only contains unit quaternions, we’ll restrict our space of points to be operated on to the unit quaternions with zero scalar part, which sit on the 2-sphere boundary between the inner core and the outer shell. That way we can visualise points moving around on our map.

It turns out to be not quite as simple and convenient as the complex numbers, but in a way that is easily fixed. First, we’ll use MATHI5c7665637b697d as our rotation, and apply it to various test quaternions using the rules we listed last time:

\[\vec{i}\vec{j} = \vec{k} \quad \quad \vec{i}\vec{k} = -\vec{j} \quad \quad \vec{i}(-\vec{j}) = -\vec{k} \quad \quad \vec{i}(-\vec{k}) = \vec{j}\]

These evidently are working as a cycle: the output of each stage becomes the input to the next stage. As MATHI5c7665637b697d, MATHI5c7665637b6a7d and MATHI5c7665637b6b7d are acting as basis vectors for 3D space, we effectively visit these points in the coordinate system, starting at MATHI5c7665637b6a7d:

\[(0, 1, 0) \quad \quad (0, 0, 1) \quad \quad (0, -1, 0) \quad \quad (0, 0, -1)\]

So looks like a very helpful rotation in the MATHI797a-plane, around the MATHI78-axis, in MATHI39305e5c63697263 increments, and certainly if the MATHI78-coordinate is zero then it stays zero. By symmetry we can similarly rotate the MATHI7a78-plane around the MATHI79-axis by multiplying repeatedly by MATHI5c7665637b6a7d, or the MATHI7879-plane around the MATHI7a-axis by multiplying repeatedly by MATHI5c7665637b6b7d.

So it sounds like we can perform rotations around all three axes, using their basis vectors. Which ever imaginary quaternion you choose to rotate by, the other two imaginary components are affected. Also by reducing the strength of the imaginary components (and making a compensating increase to the real component to keep it a unit quaternion) you can reduce the angle by which it rotates from MATHI39305e5c63697263 to whatever angle you require.

Hence, a first guess at a general formula, the angle MATHI5c7468657461 determining the mix between real and imaginary, and the imaginary part being simply a unit vector imported from 3D space:

\[r = \cos \left( \theta \right) + \sin \left( \theta \right) (u_x \vec{i} + u_y \vec{j} + u_z \vec{k})\]

But before we celebrate too much, we need to see what happens to points that aren’t on the one specific circle of points we’ve tested so far. If we apply MATHI5c7665637b697d as the operator to a test quaternion that has a non-zero MATHI5c7665637b697d component, MATHI78205c6e652030, what happens? It’s not good news. Clearly, like in regular complex numbers, if we apply MATHI5c7665637b697d to itself we get MATHI2d31, and so on:

\[\vec{i}\vec{i} = -1 \quad \quad \vec{i}(-1) = -\vec{i} \quad \quad \vec{i}(-\vec{i}) = 1 \quad \quad \vec{i}(1) = i\]

This is a rotation alright, at least in quaternion-space, but on our 3D map, referring to our test input, it looks more like a conveyor belt, carrying points in a straight line along the MATHI78-axis, passing through MATHI31 (the centre of the map), MATHI5c7665637b697d (on the equator, or the spherical boundary between the inner core and the outer shell), MATHI2d31 (the outer shell, where it teleports to the opposite side of the ball-map), continuing through MATHI2d5c7665637b697d before returning to MATHI31 and repeating the cycle.

This looks exactly like ordinary complex rotation, interchanging between the real number line and whichever imaginary component we chose to multiply by, but the effect of it on our ball-map is to drag anything not on the MATHI78203d20302c20795e32202b207a5e32203d2031 circle around in a kind of weird cycle that includes an apparently discontinuous flip from positive MATHI78 to negative MATHI78. Really of course this discontinuity is a side-effect of our projection to 3D. The unit quaternions with positive and negative MATHI78 are really two halves of the hypersphere surface.

In your mind, set the MATHI79 and MATHI7a coordinates of a test quaternion to zero, while allowing MATHI78 and MATHI77 (the real, scalar coordinate) to cycle around the surface. The test quaternion travels through the North Pole (MATHI773d312c20783d30) smoothly and without incident. Why can’t it do the same at the South Pole? It can, and does! It passes through (MATHI773d2d312c20783d30) just as smoothly. It’s just that in our projection to 3D, we exploded the South Pole into the outermost sphere, the 3D ice wall of our 3D United Nations map, where all points have coordinates MATHI28773d2d312c20783d302c20793d302c207a3d3029. So anything that passes through the South Pole appears, on our projection, to discontinuously teleport. When MATHI78 has a tiny positive value, it’s right next to the ice wall on one side of the outer sphere, and when it passes through MATHI783d30 to become slightly negative, it’s then just inside the ice wall on the opposite side.

Despite this, our projection still makes sense because the kinds of rotation we want are interchanges between imaginary pairs like MATHI6a6b, which look like well-behaved rotations in the projection space. But an interchange between an imaginary component and the real number line totally destroys this neat picture.

The one saving grace is that, because we’re always acting with unit quaternions on test subjects that are also unit quaternions, the product is always another unit quaternion, so at least they don’t disappear from the map entirely. Our map has no place for non-unit quaternions. It’s just a unit-only slice of the space of all possible quaternions, as we threw away non-unit quaternions to achieve a 3D projection. Any operation on a test quaternion that moves it away from the surface of the unit hypersphere will make it vanish entirely from our map, “into the fourth dimension”! A somewhat science-fictiony phrase that isn’t particularly helpful, because if something exists in a 4D space then obviously it has always been somewhere in the fourth dimension, just as it has always been somewhere in the other three. But it would no longer be sitting in the one 3D slice visible in our map.

So the action of a quaternion with an imaginary component, such as MATHI69, is in effect two simultaneous rotations:

  • the one we want: the quaternion MATHI69 defines an axis around which the other two imaginary components rotate, so the MATHI6a6b plane tumbles nicely around it.
  • the one we don’t want: complex real-imaginary interchange that our projection converts into cyclical discontinuous teleportation through the ice wall.

Fortunately there’s a simple trick that fixes this. Quaternion multiplication is anti-commutative:

\[\vec{i}\vec{j} = -\vec{j}\vec{i}\]

We can apply a quaternion as a rotation operator on the left side and the right, and they have different effects. What we want to do is reinforce the good rotation (involving interchange between the imaginary components) and cancel out the unhelpful rotation (involving interchange with the real, scalar component).

Let’s see what happens when we multiply a general quaternion MATHI71 on the left by MATHI5c7665637b697d:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \vec{i} q &=& \vec{i} (w + x\vec{i} + y\vec{j} + z\vec{k}) \\ &=& w\vec{i} + x\vec{i}^2 + y\vec{i}\vec{j} + z\vec{i}\vec{k} \end{eqnarray*}\]

Notice how the effect of MATHI69 on the MATHI77 coordinate, as it’s just a real, will not depend on which side we multiplied MATHI5c7665637b697d on. Real/imaginary multiplication is commutative. But also notice how the same is true for the MATHI78 coordinate, because there we just multiply MATHI5c7665637b697d by itself, so switching left and right can’t make any difference. It’s just MATHI5c7665637b697d5e32203d202d31.

Whereas for the remaining two coordinates, they now scale the products of two different imaginary units, MATHI5c7665637b697d5c7665637b6a7d203d205c7665637b6b7d and MATHI5c7665637b697d5c7665637b6b7d203d202d5c7665637b6a7d, and we know that such products are anti-commutative: switching sides would switch signs. So substituting these identities:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \vec{i} q &=& w\vec{i} - x + y\vec{k} - z\vec{j} \\ &=& -x + w\vec{i} - z\vec{j} + y\vec{k} \end{eqnarray*}\]

On that last line we just put the components in the usual order. Just to show explicitly how multiplying on the right disagrees:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} q \vec{i} &=& (w + x\vec{i} + y\vec{j} + z\vec{k}) \vec{i} \\ &=& w\vec{i} + x\vec{i}^2 + y\vec{j}\vec{i} + z\vec{k}\vec{i} \\ &=& w\vec{i} - x - y\vec{k} + z\vec{j} \\ &=& -x + w\vec{i} + z\vec{j} - y\vec{k} \end{eqnarray*}\]

We can see how the two simultaneous rotations performed by MATHI5c7665637b697d are affected by the switching of sides. Or rather, only of them is affected: the rotation in the real/MATHI5c7665637b697d-plane stays exactly the same. The other one, the useful one, is sadly reversed. This means that if we performed both actions, multiplying by MATHI5c7665637b697d on both sides:

\[\vec{i}q\vec{i}\]

then the useful MATHI5c7665637b6a7d5c7665637b6b7d-plane rotation would be undone, and the irritating crazy conveyor belt effect would be reinforced. How infuriating. But if we knew how to make the multiplicative inverse of any quaternion, that would reverse both rotations. Then then we could multiply by the inverse on the right, and we would reinforce the useful rotation and cancel the irritating one! So we just need to know how to find the inverse of a quaternion.

Hamilton already figured this stuff out with algebra. He wanted quaternions to behave like numbers, so he needed to be able to divide as well as multiply, so given a quaternion MATHI72 he wanted to find MATHI725e7b2d317d such that MATHI72725e7b2d317d203d2031. What he discovered was that, exactly like conjugation with complex numbers, we can form the conjugate of a quaternion by flipping the sign of the imaginary parts:

\[r = w + x\vec{i} + y\vec{j} + z\vec{k} \quad \quad r^* = w - x\vec{i} - y\vec{j} - z\vec{k}\]

And as you’d expect, if we multiply them, we get a purely real value, the modulus-squared:

\[r r^* = w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2\]

So to scale this back to MATHI31, we just need to divide by the modulus-squared, giving:

\[r^{-1} = \frac{r^*}{|r|^2}\]

But we’re describing rotations with unit quaternions, so the modulus is always MATHI31, and thus for our purposes we can use conjugation to get the inverse. This is extremely reminiscent of how the inverse of a unitary operator in matrix form can be found by the conjugate transpose, isn’t it?

So to perform a rotation by MATHI72, on the left we use MATHI72 and on the right we use its conjugate, MATHI725e2a, which can be found by flipping the signs of all the imaginary terms in MATHI72. This cancels out the unwanted conveyor belt effect along the direction of MATHI72, leaving just the desired proper rotation in the plane perpendicular to MATHI72’s vector part. Although now we’ve applied that rotation twice, and this explains the factor of MATHI312f32 on the angle in the formula for building a general quaternion to rotate by:

\[r = \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) (u_x \vec{i} + u_y \vec{j} + u_z \vec{k})\]

So the full recipe to use MATHI72 to rotate a point in 3D space is as follows. Represent that point MATHI70 as a quaternion using the imaginary units to carry the point’s coordinates:

\[p = p_x \vec{i} + p_y \vec{j} + p_z \vec{k}\]

and then make a sandwich:

\[p^\prime = r p r^*\]

where MATHI725e2a is just MATHI72 with a minus sign on the vector terms, i.e.

\[r = \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) - \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) (u_x \vec{i} + u_y \vec{j} + u_z \vec{k})\]

This is probably enough mid-18th century geometry for now.

entry.title: Quantumania 24 - Learn from the Flerfers
entry.content:
The quaternions were discovered by Hamilton in 1843 when he was trying to figure out how to extend complex numbers to span three dimensions. He realised he needed four dimensions to make it work. He wasn’t thinking in terms of matrices, or even vectors. He just created two more special values alongside MATHI31 and MATHI69. And 84 years later, Pauli wasn’t thinking of quaternions when he followed the rules of QM to come up with his matrices, although others spotted the resemblance immediately.

Before seeing how they work, we’ll temporarily jump forwards into what is certainly the most important application of quaternions: rotations in three dimensions, just because it will convey just how much they resonate with our findings about qubits. Check out how a quaternion, MATHI72, representing a rotation by angle MATHI5c7468657461 around an axis MATHI5c7665637b757d, is built from the component quaternions scaled by the coordinates of the axis, MATHI5c7665637b757d203d2028755f782c20755f792c20755f7a29:

\[r = \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) (u_x \vec{i} + u_y \vec{j} + u_z \vec{k})\]

Although we haven’t looked at it yet, this is basically identical to the formula for making a matrix representing a rotation around such an axis by composing the Pauli matrices. But also:

  • Look at how the angles are being halved, exactly like angles in the qubit state space compared with the angles in Bloch/physical space.
  • As a result, if you add MATHI325c7069 to MATHI5c7468657461, you get MATHI2d72, because the angle is halved, so MATHI5c636f73 and MATHI5c73696e only go through half a cycle. You need to add another MATHI3336305e5c63697263 to get back to MATHI72. This is exactly the same thing that happens with qubits.
  • But the quaternions MATHI72 and MATHI2d72 perform the same rotation, because if the axis is pointing the opposite way and you switch from clockwise to anticlockwise rotation at the same time, those two changes cancel out. That is, the two quaternions have the same physical interpretation, which is reminiscent of how quantum states represent the same physical state under a sign flip.
  • We’ll also see how quaternions have the pleasant symmetry of representing both operations-on-things and things-being-operated-on by the same objects, just like when we use a density operator to represent the state of a qubit.

But the really fun thing about quaternions, I think, is that to get an intuitive understanding of how they model rotations in 3D, we can learn a thing or two from those lovable fools, the flat earthers! In particular, their obsession with a particular projection of the globe onto the plane, called the azimuthal equidistant projection. This is map of the earth that appears on the flag of the United Nations, sometimes described as a “view from above”, which really doesn’t do it justice.

Imagine you live on a ball of radius ~6360 km. This shouldn’t be too hard, because you do. As you are tiny, less than a ten millionth of that radius, at your local scale the surface of the ball appears to be flat, as long as you don’t stare too long at the horizon and notice what happens to tall ships as they disappear from view. So it seems reasonable to make a flat map of the surface with the outlines of all the countries on it, starting from wherever you are and working outwards. The challenge comes from the distortion that occurs as you get further away from your chosen starting point, and there is no one right or best way to deal with this. Every such projection has drawbacks.

Following the example of the UN, we will be northern-hemisphere-centric and put the North Pole at the middle of our map of the world. We’ll surround that point with concentric circles representing the circles of constant latitude on the globe. Each is a set of points that are all the same distance (travelling on the surface) from the North Pole. There is an intuitive relationship going on: as the circles we add to our map get larger, so do the circles they represent on the globe.

At some point we’ll reach the equator, which is just another circle on our map, but in terms of the relationship between the actual globe and our map, it marks a significant boundary: if we keep going, the concentric circles on our map continue to get larger (they’re still getting further from the North Pole) but the corresponding circles of constant latitude on the globe are now getting smaller, as they get closer to the South Pole. This has a severe distorting effect on how the southern hemisphere is represented: on the UN flag Australia looks like a sausage.

Finally, when we reach the South Pole itself, the distortion is ridiculous: the South Pole isn’t a point on our map. Instead it’s the largest outermost circle at the edge, twice the radius of the equator’s circle. This is where the flat earthers say that the continent of Antarctica, far from being a landmass that encloses the South Pole, is instead a giant circular wall of ice, which is why the authorities never allow anyone to visit it.

The things to note here are that we took a ball in 3D space, we ignored everything about that space except for the surface of the ball, which is to say, a sphere, and we poked a hole in the bottom and unwrapped the surface by stretching the hole out to a circle, which is the outermost boundary of a surface with the top of the sphere sitting in the middle. This is possible because a sphere (the surface of a ball) is inherently 2-dimensional, which is why its official name is a 2-sphere. The points in the 3D space, identified by MATHI28782c20792c207a29 coordinates, with MATHI28302c20302c203029 being the centre of the ball, include a subset for which:

\[x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\]

These are just the points exactly on the unit sphere, nothing inside it (the rest of the ball) and nothing in outer space. So for example, the North Pole has coordinates MATHI28302c20302c203129 (MATHI7a being the north-south axis of the globe), and that’s the middle of our UN-style map, so at the middle, the MATHI7a-coordinate is MATHI31, precisely because the other two are zero, so it has to be MATHI31 to satisfy our formula. Meanwhile all the points on our map that sit on the outer circle, where the South Pole ended up stretched out into the “ice wall”, they paradoxically all have the coordinates MATHI28302c20302c202d3129. The equator, meanwhile, is actually a sensible circle on both the actual sphere and on our map, so its coordinates are any points MATHI28782c20792c203029, where:

\[x^2 + y^2 = 1\]

So as we move out from the centre of our map to the outer circle, the MATHI7a value starts at MATHI31 (North Pole), goes down to MATHI30 (equator) and finally reaches MATHI2d31 (South Pole). The other two coordinates are able to vary as points on a circle, making up whatever is left over after MATHI7a5e32 has supplied its share of the total that must be MATHI31.

This means that MATHI78 and MATHI79 are the only true coordinates, as you’d expect on a 2D map. If you pin them down, MATHI7a can only have one of two possible values:

\[z = \pm \sqrt{1 - (x^2 + y^2)}\]

So it isn’t a free coordinate on our map, and doesn’t play any role in how the space of the map operates. It’s just a shadow of the 3D space that the actual sphere lives in.

One important scenario to have clear is the journey taken by an airliner if it sets of from the central North Pole and heads toward the South pole (which is to say, in any direction, because all directions lead to the South Pole.) What happens to the airliner as viewed on our map when it reaches the ice wall? It teleports to the opposite side of the circle and then carries on going. This magic trick is of course merely an artefact of how the projection works, unwrapping the southern hemisphere and stretching the pole out into a circle. In reality the airliner just cruises over the South Pole without so much as a glitch, presumably to the great annoyance of any flerfers on board.

Now suppose we replicate this situation but starting with a 4-dimensional space of points MATHI28772c20782c20792c207a29. We cannot visualise this, which is a problem. But suppose this space contains a 4-ball centred on its origin, whose surface is therefore a 3-sphere (yes, a three-dimensional “surface”, just go with it!), which is all the points in the space where:

\[w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\]

Just as before, by constraining our interest to a subset of the space, we cut the number of dimensions by 1, and thus we have a way to make a map of the 3D “surface” of a 4D ball. And we can visualise in 3D, so we’re back in business. We just need to make the 3D version of the UN’s map of the world, by “flattening” (relatively speaking) that surface into a 3-ball. The circles of the UN map will become spheres in our new map.

This time the MATHI77 coordinate will be the direction we’ll flatten along, and we have a clear reason to treat it as different to the other three. Our four coordinates are the parameters of a general quaternion:

\[q = w + x\vec{i} + y\vec{j} + z\vec{k}\]

The MATHI77 coordinate is the real part. The other three coordinates scale the imaginary units, and we will treat them as orthogonal directions in familiar physical space. Each point within our 3D ball map has a single unit quaternion associated with it. The MATHI77 coordinate is therefore not an independent unconstrained parameter: it just has to compensate for the other three to bring the total of all their squares to MATHI31.

Once again we start at the North Pole, now along the MATHI77 axis, coordinates: MATHI28312c20302c20302c203029. Here the other three coordinates must be zero, because MATHI77 is already contributing MATHI315e32 to the sum in the constraining formula. We are on top of the world in 4D, but this point sits in the very core of our solid ball-map. In the 3D space map space, if we move to nearby points, then MATHI77 will have to shrink from MATHI31 to accommodate the MATHI28782c20792c207a29 coordinates taking on non-zero values.

Eventually this exploration of the surrounding space will take us to the equator, which in our solid map is a sphere, and is the set of points where MATHI77 has fallen to exactly MATHI30, while the other three coordinates obey:

\[x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\]

This is also the boundary between the northern and southern hemispheres of the 3-sphere we’re mapping. But of course, as before, as far as our map is concerned, it’s just a concentric 2-sphere. We can continue exploring the southern hemisphere, where MATHI77 falls below zero and eventually reaches MATHI2d31, so the other three coordinates must shrink to accommodate it. At this point, we have a final outermost concentric 2-sphere in our map, the “ice wall”, on which every point is the South Pole and has the coordinates MATHI282d312c20302c20302c203029.

So, every point inside the ice wall represents a point on the surface of a 3-sphere in 4D quaternion-space. The 3D ball of our solid map can be divided into two parts, an inner core ball, like the Earth’s molten iron core, corresponding to points on the northern hemisphere of the actual 3-sphere, where MATHI77203e2030, and an outer shell, like the Earth’s mantle, which is the southern hemisphere of the 3-sphere, where MATHI77203c2030.

The points inside our ball-map consists of all the unit quaternions:

\[\vec{q} = w + x\vec{i} + y\vec{j} + z\vec{k} \quad \quad w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\]

The real part MATHI77 is called the scalar and the other three comprise the vector part of the quaternion. It was actually Hamilton who came up with these terms, which were later borrowed when vector spaces were abstracted out of his work.

Now we’ve constructed our solid United Nations map of all unit quaternions, what are we going to use it for?

He realised he needed four dimensions to make it work. He wasn’t thinking in terms of matrices, or even vectors. He just created two more special values alongside $1$ and $i$. And 84 years later, Pauli wasn’t thinking of quaternions when he followed the rules of QM to come up with his matrices, although others spotted the resemblance immediately.

entry.title: Quantumania 23 - Turn! Turn! Turn!
entry.content:
The reflections MATHI58, MATHI59, MATHI5a were figured out by Pauli, who started with some basic constraints imposed by what was already known in 1927 (a pretty important year in QM.) First, it was known since 1922’s Stern-Gerlach experiment that if you put a beam of silver atoms through a linear magnetic gradient, they behave as if every atom is a little bar magnet (a unit of magnetic moment) that is aligned exactly with the gradient, one way or the other. Half of them go up, half go down, the beam is split so makes two bright dots on the screen. This was surprising because you’d assume from classical intuition that they would fan out, each atom having a random orientation relative to the gradient.

Second, Dirac had already explained that in QM, if a quantum system has a measurable property with two possible outcomes, the vector state space for that system is two dimensional. Putting these first two concepts together, the state space describing the orientation of a particle’s magnetic moment must be two dimensional.

Third, by feeding the “up” output particle beam from the above experiment into exactly the same kind of apparatus, but with the magnetic gradient rotated MATHI39305e5c63697263, the beam splits again, left/right. This makes sense if you think of each particle’s magnetic moment as a dot on a sphere, and each of these stages acting as a filter that only allows through particles whose dot is in one of the two hemispheres, divided by an equator that depends on the alignment of the magnetic gradient. If the particles’s dots are randomly distributed over the sphere of possible spatial directions, only half of them have their dot in the upper hemisphere, and then of that beam, only half qualify as right hemisphere, and so on. The second stage’s rightward beam must, you’d naively think, therefore contain only particles whose dot is in the upper-right quarter (they’ve made it through both filters.)

And so a third stage aligned to split up/down again should only produce a single up beam. But it produces two equal beams, up and down. From this we are forced to conclude that each stage, when treated as a filter, has the effect of snapping every particle into alignment with its field gradient, one way or the other, and that therefore the second stage wipes out the alignments produced by the first stage. Also there seems to be a random choice made for each particle as to which way to snap into alignment.

Again, Dirac had already established the rules of QM here: the two dimensional (complex) state space for particle alignment has to represent mutually exclusive measurement outcomes, such as up/down, with orthogonal vectors, and other (incompatible) observable outcomes, such as left/right, must be expressible as a sum of up/down, and vice versa. Also observables correspond to self-adjoint operators (Hermitian matrices). With these rules in place, and the results of Stern-Gerlach, Pauli found that there was exactly one way to arrange the state vectors for three orthogonal spatial directions, and the operators for the observables corresponding to those directions are the three reflections around MATHI5c6b65747b307d, MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d and MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d, which are MATHI58, MATHI59 and MATHI5a respectively.

Now, the first thing to notice about Pauli’s three matrices is that they are traceless. This means that the sum of their eigenvalues is zero, as they are QM operators, thus self-adjoint, thus normal, which is to say amenable to being diagonalised, in which form they are all just MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b646961677d28312c202d3129. They can be linearly combined to represent any alignment in space, to make Hamiltonians (energy operators) that steer the evolution of a particle’s spin orientation.

But any such combination will also have zero trace (the trace is a linear operator, so the trace of a sum of matrices is the sum of their individual traces). Therefore we can’t make any old matrix with these three ingredients, only those that possess this particular quality of balanced eigenvalues on either side of zero. We can’t make a matrix with eigenvalues MATHI28312c203029, for example. This inability of three matrices to span the space of all possible MATHI32205c74696d65732032 matrices is hardly surprising: it’s clearly a 4-dimensional space, so we need a forth ingredient, one that acts as a kind of “unit of trace”, a constant to be added to all the diagonal entries to offset their total away from zero. This ingredient is simply MATHI49. But physically the significance of energy levels is the difference between them, so we don’t usually require this ingredient to model an actual Hamiltonian. Balancing the energy levels around zero is neat and symmetrical. It’s just interesting to note that MATHI49 is theoretically one of the four ingredients alongside MATHI58, MATHI59 and MATHI5a, even if our interest in its involvement falls away rapidly when we realise what its role would be.

But there is another role for MATHI49 in combination with the other Pauli matrices. Recall how every state has a second way of being represented, as a density matrix. This means that every point on the Bloch sphere, being a definite state, corresponds to a density matrix. The rules for density matrices are:

  • They must be Hermitian, so their eigenvalues are real, because they are probabilities.
  • The eigenvalues must also be non-negative, for the same reason.
  • If diagonalised (as they always can be in some basis) their eigenvalues appear on the diagonal, and being an exhaustive set of probabilities, they must sum to MATHI31, which is to say that the trace must be MATHI31.

Now, by a weighted sum of the three Pauli matrices MATHI58, MATHI59, MATHI5a, each having their own real weighting coefficient MATHI78, MATHI79, MATHI7a, we are able to make a matrix corresponding any point on the Bloch sphere:

\[xX + yY + zZ\]

The real coordinates MATHI28782c20792c207a29 specify a point anywhere in 3D space, but we want to only target the surface of the unit sphere, so we require MATHI785e32202b20795e32202b207a5e32203d2031. But as noted, the trace of any such combination will be 0, as the eigenvalues will always be MATHI31 and MATHI2d31. So it’s not yet a valid density matrix. But this is where MATHI49 comes to the rescue!

\[I + xX + yY + zZ\]

We’ve added a unit of “positive trace” to the diagonal, so now the eigenvalues are MATHI302c2032. So close! We need to scale them down to MATHI302c2031:

\[\rho = \frac{1}{2} (I + xX + yY + zZ) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1+z & x-iy \\ x+iy & 1-z \end{bmatrix}\]

The second thing to notice is that while MATHI58, MATHI59 and MATHI5a act as reflections in the state space, this is not what they do on the Bloch sphere. As always, this is an area ripe for confusion. Recall that MATHI5a flips the sign on MATHI5c6b65747b317d only:

\[Z\ket{0} = \ket{0} \quad \quad Z\ket{1} = -\ket{1}\]

On the Bloch sphere, these two vectors are the up/down poles, and of course a sign flip doesn’t move anything. So on the sphere, MATHI5a has no effect at all on these two states. They stay put. What happens to MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d and MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d, which sit on the front/back poles? They actually switch places:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Exactly the same thing happens with MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d and MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d, unsurprisingly. So this is in fact a MATHI3138305e5c63697263 rotation around the MATHI5a-axis. Each matrix, while being a simple reflection in state space, is a rotation in physical space. But because it’s a MATHI3138305e5c63697263 rotation, applying it twice in succession will restore the starting state, which is consistent with a reflection in state space. By constructing a linear combination of the three we can make a rotational axis in any direction we require.

The third thing to notice is what happens when you multiply the three directional matrices together in certain pairs with ordinary matrix multiplication:

\[XY = iZ \quad \quad YZ = iX \quad \quad ZX = iY\]

Seemingly any pair is a way to make the remaining one, well, almost, apart from that MATHI69 factor. Though if you flip the order, it introduces a minus sign:

\[YX = -iZ \quad \quad ZY = -iX \quad \quad XZ = -iY\]

And here is an interesting thing. Define the following mystery objects:

\[\vec{i} = -iX \quad \quad \vec{j} = -iY \quad \quad \vec{k} = -iZ \quad \quad\]

That is, each is just a Pauli matrix multiplied by MATHI2d69. For completeness we’ll give a new symbol to the identity operator:

\[\vec{1} = I\]

What happens when we square them? It’s just matrix multiplication, and we know the Pauli matrices are self-inverse:

\[X^2 = Y^2 = Z^2 = I\]

So the extra MATHI2d69 factor produces MATHI2d31:

\[\vec{i}^2 = \vec{j}^2 = \vec{k}^2 = -\vec{1}\]

And if you multiply pairs of them, the extra factor preserves itself:

\[\vec{i}\vec{j} = (-iX)(-iY) = -XY = -iZ = \vec{k}\]

Or to tabulate all pairings systematically:

\[\vec{i}\vec{j} = \vec{k} \quad \quad \vec{j}\vec{k} = \vec{i} \quad \quad \vec{k}\vec{i} = \vec{j}\] \[\vec{j}\vec{i} = -\vec{k} \quad \quad \vec{k}\vec{j} = -\vec{i} \quad \quad \vec{i}\vec{k} = -\vec{j}\]

and for good measure (by simple substitution from the above discoveries):

\[\vec{i} \vec{j} \vec{k} = -\vec{1}\]

The curious thing is that if you start from a very simple premise, you can derive these rules and they work exactly like the Pauli matrices.
entry.summary: The reflections $X$, $Y$, $Z$ were figured out by Pauli, who started with some basic constraints imposed by what was already known in 1927 (a pretty important year in QM.) First, it was known since 1922’s Stern-Gerlach experiment that if you put a beam of silver atoms through a linear magnetic gradient, they behave as if every atom is a little bar magnet (a unit of magnetic moment) that is aligned exactly with the gradient, one way or the other. Half of them go up, half go down, the beam is split so makes two bright dots on the screen. This was surprising because you’d assume from classical intuition that they would fan out, each atom having a random orientation relative to the gradient.

entry.title: Quantumania 22 - Three Dimensions
entry.content:
When we first looked at the Hadamard gate there arose three matrices representing directions in physical space. They were introduced a little abruptly like background characters in someone else’s story, and they deserve some more spotlight. Here they are again:

\[Z = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \quad X = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad Y = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Geometrically they are all simply reflections. This is most obvious in MATHI5a, because they’re all written in the MATHI5a basis. MATHI5a just flips the sign of the second coordinate (the one that scales MATHI5c6b65747b317d) and has no effect on the first coordinate (the one that scales MATHI5c6b65747b307d). Or to put it another way, a vector of the form MATHI635c6b65747b307d, where MATHI63 is any complex scalar, is entirely unaffected:

\[Z c\ket{0} = c\ket{0}\]

whereas a vector of the form MATHI635c6b65747b317d experiences a sign-flip:

\[Z c\ket{1} = -c\ket{1}\]

So these, being only scaled by MATHI5a, are the eigenvectors of MATHI5a, whereas any other vectors will not only be scaled, they will be re-aligned. In general any state vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d can be written:

\[\ket{\psi} = a\ket{0} + b\ket{1}\]

The probability of measuring state MATHI5c6b65747b307d is MATHI61615e2a203d207c617c5e32, and for MATHI5c6b65747b317d it’s MATHI62625e2a203d207c627c5e32. But the act of multiplying (say) MATHI61 by its own complex conjugate has the effect of erasing any overall complex phase, because:

\[\left( e^{i\theta} \right)^* = e^{-i\theta}\]

and:

\[e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta} = e^{i\theta-i\theta} = e^0 = 1\]

This means that although MATHI5a flips the sign of MATHI5c6b65747b317d, this does not constitute an effect on anything physically significant about the state, because a sign flip is just a phase factor.

The other matrices represent the two orthogonal directions to MATHI5a. MATHI58 swaps the coordinates between MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d, performing a reflection around the MATHI34355e5c63697263 line lying between them. This is the line that MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d sits on (if you’ve read the previous entries, you’ll be familiar with the diagram by now.) So MATHI5a has no effect at all on MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, meaning that here MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d plays the same role that MATHI5c6b65747b307d played under MATHI5a. Likewise, a vector aligned with MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d would flip to point the opposite way. So if we were to rewrite all these matrices in the MATHI58 basis, then the MATHI58 matrix would have that same simple MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b646961677d28312c202d3129 form that we’ve given to the MATHI5a matrix.

MATHI59 is apparently the most exciting, in that it seems to combine both ingredients seen so far: a sign difference between the coordinates (like MATHI5a) and a swapping between the coordinates (off-diagonal entries only, like MATHI58), but to these it adds an overall factor of MATHI69. Again we can see how it affects its eigenvectors, which are given the mnemonic labels MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d and MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d to remind us of the coordinate on MATHI5c6b65747b317d:

\[\ket{+i} = \frac{\ket{0} + i\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \quad \ket{-i} = \frac{\ket{0} - i\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\]

Visualising this geometrically at first seems next to impossible (the MATHI5c6b65747b317d component has been scaled by a complex rotation that nevertheless doesn’t change its alignment), but based on the pattern so far, we’d expect MATHI59 to have no effect on MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d (we can ignore the overall MATHI5c667261637b317d7b5c737172747b327d7d because it appears on both sides of the equation):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

Check! Whereas it should perform an overall MATHI2d31 scale on MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ i \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

All is as expected. In fact we can visualise it geometrically if we just relabel the axes on our usual diagram (come on, it’s been a while). When we use the MATHI5a-basis unit vectors MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d to express the eigenvectors of MATHI58, we quietly ignored MATHI59, leaving it off the diagram. Well, now we can switch allegiance:

What is this voodoo?! Actually we’re still technically in the MATHI5a-basis here, because our vertical axis MATHI695c6b65747b317d is just as much of a valid eigenvector of MATHI5a as is MATHI5c6b65747b317d. Our diagrams have to be real subspaces of MATHI5c6d61746862627b437d5e32. We normally draw the real subspace spanned by MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c205c6b65747b317d205c726272616365, now we’re using the real subspace spanned by MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c20695c6b65747b317d205c726272616365.

In Bloch sphere terms, it gets even simpler. First, think of the usual MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c205c6b65747b317d205c726272616365 diagram. It is easily visualised as a circular slice through the Bloch sphere (with one important caveat). If you follow a point moving around that circle, it visits MATHI5c6b65747b307d, MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, MATHI5c6b65747b317d, MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d in that order. Or to use their physical-space names instead of computing names, MATHI5c6b65747b757d (up), MATHI5c6b65747b667d (front), MATHI5c6b65747b647d (down), MATHI5c6b65747b627d (back):

There is no way to access MATHI5c6b65747b6c7d (left) MATHI5c6b65747b727d (right) from the provided ingredients if you are restricted to using only real coordinates to scale them. It’s the MATHI58-MATHI5a great circle, no MATHI59 ingredients are supplied, so the rest of the sphere is out of bounds. The caveat I mentioned is that the circle on the flat state space diagram is not precisely the same circle as this slice through the Bloch sphere, because MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d are orthogonal in the state space, whereas in the corresponding Block sphere great circle they are antipodes (on opposite sides). The angle separating any two states is doubled on the Bloch sphere.

Now with MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c20695c6b65747b317d205c726272616365 as the axes of our state space diagram, we can access a great circle that visits MATHI5c6b65747b307d, MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d, MATHI695c6b65747b317d205c70726f70746f205c6b65747b317d, MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d, or MATHI5c6b65747b757d, MATHI5c6b65747b727d, MATHI5c6b65747b647d, MATHI5c6b65747b6c7d, never MATHI5c6b65747b667d or MATHI5c6b65747b627d. It’s MATHI59-MATHI5a only, and has no MATHI58 ingredients for us to scale with our strictly real coordinates:

Note how the state diagram’s MATHI695c6b65747b317d only differs by a phase factor (MATHI2d31) from MATHI5c6b65747b317d, so these refer to the same point on the Bloch sphere.

We’ve still only scratched the surface of this topic. For example, the matrices are reflections in 2-dimensional complex state space. What are they in the Bloch sphere, that is, in real 3-dimensional physical space?

entry.title: Quantumania 21 - Slot Machines
entry.content:
A ket is a “regular” vector, from the vector space MATHI56, a bra is a covector from the dual space MATHI565e2a (here I think QM has the upper hand, because almost everything is a vector, so it helps to have a specific term for a “regular” vector.)

A covector MATHI66 is a black box machine with one slot in the top, and you insert a vector MATHI5c7665637b617d, and out pops a scalar MATHI78:

It’s linear:

\[f(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = f(\vec{a}) + f(\vec{b}) \quad \quad f(x \vec{a}) = x f(\vec{a})\]

We can add such machines (make a machine with one input slot, and internally it just feeds a copy of that input to two hidden machines and then sums their output scalars to produce the final output). Likewise we can scale a machine. The space of all such possible machines is a vector space MATHI565e2a. In QM we write such a machine as MATHI5c6272617b667d and have it operate on a vector MATHI5c6b65747b617d like this: MATHI5c6272616b65747b667d7b617d, and we define a one-to-one mapping between bras and kets. In general, that asterisk notation MATHI565e2a for the dual space of a space MATHI56 has nothing to do with complex conjugates. It’s a neat coincidence that the bra-ket mapping in a QM state space involves complex conjugation.

We can also make a machine with two slots, accepting vectors MATHI5c7665637b617d and MATHI5c7665637b627d, but still with one output hole that gives us back a scalar MATHI78:

Suppose that this two-slot machine had an especially simple inner mechanism: inside the box MATHI68 there are two single-slot boxes (covectors) MATHI66 and MATHI67. The machinery inserts input MATHI5c7665637b617d into box MATHI66, and input MATHI5c7665637b627d into box MATHI67, to obtain two scalars, which it simply multiplies together to produce its own resultant scalar that falls out of the hole of MATHI68. In other words, it’s really just two covectors glued together by scalar multiplication, and they act independently on the inputs. We can think of the tensor product on the input vectors as gluing them together in a specific order so it’s clear which slot each one is meant to go in:

\[\bra{h} = \bra{f} \otimes \bra{g}\] \[\bra{h} \Big( \ket{a} \otimes \ket{b} \Big) = \Big( \bra{f} \otimes \bra{g} \Big) \Big( \ket{a} \otimes \ket{b} \Big) = \braket{f}{a} \cdot \braket{g}{b}\]

This is a product machine, it’s behaviour explicable in terms of two separate inner machines. This is not true of all two-slot machines. Once again, these are vectors from a combined vector space, MATHI565e2a205c6f74696d657320565e2a. We can add a pair of two-slot machines to make another two-slot machine. Thus any two-slot machine might not be separable into two one-slot machines. It may only be expressible as the sum of multiple product machines. Or in QM terms:

\[\bra{\psi} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \bra{01} - \frac{1}{2} \bra{10}\]

The MATHI5c6272617b30317d203d205c6272617b307d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b317d and MATHI5c6272617b31307d203d205c6272617b317d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b307d are product machines, but their sum is not.

Note that it isn’t necessary to provide both inputs at once. Such a two-slot machine can be given one input, say for the first slot, which clogs up that slot, resulting in what is in effect a one-slot machine. Generalising further, the scalar that falls out after both inputs are provided is, in a sense, a zero-slot machine!

The symmetry of the notation where a bra acts on a ket to produce a scalar, MATHI5c6272616b65747b667d7b617d, can just as well be read as the ket acting on the bra; when implemented as a calculation in terms of coordinates, it has the same machinery as the familiar dot product: coordinate-wise multiplication to produce terms in a sum. So you can completely flip the picture around and visualise a ket as a one-slot machine that takes a bra as its input, and the tensor product of two kets as a two-slot machine, and so on.

We can even stitch together a two-slot machine from MATHI56205c6f74696d657320565e2a, that is, being defined conceptually through the combining of a ket and a bra (in that order), its inputs need to be a bra and a ket (again, in that order).

Wait a second… this is the shape of a projection operator! The QM notation MATHI5c6b65747b617d5c6272617b627d is itself a shorthand for MATHI5c6b65747b617d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b627d. When we write:

\[\ket{a}\braket{b}{c}\]

This is the operator MATHI5c6b65747b617d5c6272617b627d acting on the ket MATHI5c6b65747b637d, or we can say it’s the ket MATHI5c6b65747b637d being inserted into the second slot of the two-slot machine MATHI5c6b65747b617d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b627d.

So a term written like this in QM notation:

\[\ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1}\]

is building a four-slot machine. The two qubits MATHI41, MATHI42 have their own vector spaces MATHI565f41, MATHI565f42, so the four-slot machine is from the space:

\[V_A \otimes V_A^* \otimes V_B \otimes V_B^*\]

Now, given that the slots of these machines are either ket-shaped, expecting to be fed a bra, or bra-shaped and expecting to be fed a ket, its not that far-fetched to suppose that you could connect one of the slots to another! They just need to be slots of the opposite type, from the same dual-space pair, such as MATHI565f42 and MATHI565f425e2a, connected by a logical pipe of some kind. This is the so-called partial trace.

Once we adopt this way of thinking, we can completely forget about matrices altogether. There’s really only one bit of notation from classical physics (GR) that we haven’t yet borrowed, and it’s awfully tempting. Cast your mind all the way back to when we wrote our joint state’s density operator as:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l}\]

I made a big deal of how I’d written the indices clustered in a certain way to get across how they relate to which system versus bra/ket. There’s already a way to do this properly. The object MATHI5c72686f holding the coefficients for the MATHI3136 possible four-slot machines can be written:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l}\]

The indices are written “up” or “down” to signify the type of object they label, up for a ket and down for a bra. The way they’re laid means we can read one row at a time to separate ket from bra indices, or instead read columns (albeit slightly staggered) to group by qubit subsystem. It’s just a labelled collection of MATHI3136 numbers, with no inherent hierarchical matrix-of-matrices structure. We can slice it however it suits us.

Of course to interpret it properly we need to use each of these coefficients to scale a basis element, and rather than writing MATHI5c6b65747b697d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b6b7d205c6f74696d6573205c6b65747b6a7d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b6c7d, we can represent a basis regular vector (ket) by MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69 (index down) and a basis covector (bra) by MATHI5c7665637b657d5e6a (index up). This opposing convention, where a coefficient and its corresponding basis element have oppositely positioned indices, has a purpose, which we’re about to get to.

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l} \Big( \vec{e}_i \otimes \vec{e}^k \otimes \vec{e}_j \otimes \vec{e}^l \Big)\]

The final ingredients are the summation symbols, but here we come to what Einstein jokingly called his only contribution to mathematics. In an expression like the above where the same index appears twice, once up and once down, this automatically implies summation over that index. So the above expression is in fact the complete equivalent of our original way of writing it. The summation over all four indices is implied, so no need to write MATHI5c73756d at all.

We can go a step further and use abstract tensor notation, also known as the slot naming convention. This means we interpret MATHI5c72686f5c696e64696365737b5e695f6b5e6a5f6c7d not as merely a collection of labelled numeric coefficients, but as the full geometric object, the four-slot machine, silently agreeing to imagine that it has the MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c646f7473 part built into it.

With this understanding, we’re writing the whole density operator for our two-qubit system as:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l}\]

Not only is this remarkably compact, it also means that if we want to “trace out” the second qubit, we just tie together its indices, which sit in the second column, by using the same symbol MATHI6a for both:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_j} = (\rho_A)\indices{^i_k}\]

Because the MATHI6a index label appears once up and once down, it is summed over, eliminating those two slots, and this is precisely the same thing as the partial trace. We’re left with the density operator for qubit MATHI41, MATHI5c72686f5f41.

The implied basis vector factor MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6b205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5f6a205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6a, also has the repeated MATHI6a index, and MATHI5c7665637b657d5f6a205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6a is equivalent to the identity operator, because it is summed over, and each term in the sum contributes a MATHI31 to the diagonal in the matrix representation, so it too disappears, leaving only the implied MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6b factor, exactly as required.

Let’s sum up. A density operator, MATHI5c72686f, can be simplistically viewed as a two-slot machine, where the slots accept a bra and a ket. Why such a pair? Taken together, they represent an input that accepts a density operator that acts as a kind of question to be asked.

So in the usual QM notation, we can write:

\[x = \bra{\phi} \rho \ket{\psi}\]

and MATHI78 is a scalar. Why the sandwich? Because the QM notation pays tribute to the pattern of matrix multiplication and the pieces have to be written in that order for such a multiplication to work. If we instead used explicit index notation:

\[x = \rho\indices{^j_k} \phi_j \psi^k\]

then we could write the factors in any order. The pairing of the indices describes a topological “wiring up” between connection points. Interpreting the factors as labelled coefficients, they are just numbers being multiplied, so clearly the order is unimportant. What matters is which combinations are multiplied and then summed. The result MATHI78 is still a scalar, because of the implied summation.

To supply a density operator to the slots is to ask a question. If we supply MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d5c6272617b5c7068697d, that’s a simple projection operator representing a specific state, and the question is: “What’s the probability that the system is in this state?” and MATHI78 is the answer.

The deeper point is that this two-slot case, while a valid way to describe any complex system, is a simplification if we are interested in the subsystems that comprise that complex system. Each subsystem can be thought of as having its own bra-ket pair of slots, and we can eliminate one subsystem by tying its slots together.

These two viewpoints are perfectly compatible because the tensor product allows us to connect the state spaces of any group of subsystems together into one state space. We can group them into a hierarchy, deal with them individually or all at once. If our system contains MATHI3130 qubits, we can divide them into three registers of MATHI32, MATHI33 and MATHI35 qubits each, each register exposing two slots. It’s vital to remember that they might not be three independent machines: their behaviour maybe correlated by entanglement.

entry.title: Quantumania 20 - Disentanglement
entry.content:
QM says the state of an isolated physical system is a well-defined thing, which I’ve characterised as sharp and definite, rather than blurry and uncertain, and which we’ve found two ways to represent: a vector in the state space, or a projection operator on that state space:

\[\ket{\psi} \quad \iff \quad \ket{\psi} \bra{\psi}\]

We can use the measurement operator for some measurement outcome (which can be as simple as the projection operator for the corresponding post-measurement state) to find the probability of an outcome, but that’s all. This implies some intrinsic uncertainty in how the universe works, sometimes called ontological probability, because the probability is aspect of the world, rather than just being due to our own lack of knowledge, which would be epistemic probability. If we attempt to measure some property, and the present state is not one of the post-measurement states associated with that property, we will nevertheless get a definite answer corresponding to one of the property’s post-measurement states, and it seems that nature chooses that answer at random. This is, in a sense, our own fault for asking the wrong question.

But the moment we measure an isolated system, it ceases to be isolated. Indeed, you could say that it never was isolated, as we were there the whole time too, along with the measuring equipment, all just subsystems of some larger system. This led us to consider composite state spaces accessed via the tensor product, which in turn led to the awkward realisation that sometimes the definite state of the composite system did not contain definite states for its subsystems. Only if the composite system is in a product state, meaning the tensor product of the states of the subsystems, can we regard the subsystem as having definite states of their own. To keep it much simpler than trying to model the state of ourselves, we’ll stick to just two qubits:

\[\ket{0} \otimes \ket{1} = \ket{01}\]

This is a product state, and is equivalent to saying that the first qubit is in MATHI5c6b65747b307d and the second is in MATHI5c6b65747b317d, so they can be thought of as possessing their own states. But this is a vector space; the sum of two vectors is also a vector, and so is also a physically real state, such as:

\[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \ket{01} - \frac{1}{2} \ket{10}\]

It can’t be rewritten as a product, in any basis. It’s inherently the sum of two product states. It is possible for you to know exactly the state this whole system was prepared in, and yet still not know what state the individual qubits are in, not because of epistemic uncertainty, but because the two qubits don’t have a state of their own. There is nothing certain for you to know. The probability of measuring MATHI5c6b65747b30317d is MATHI332f34, and there’s a MATHI312f34 chance of measuring MATHI5c6b65747b31307d. This means that if you only measured the first qubit, MATHI332f34 times it’s MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI312f34 it’s MATHI5c6b65747b317d.

Here’s where the idea of a mixed state really becomes useful. We introduced it by considering boring old epistemic uncertainty, a coin flip whose result Bob doesn’t know. But we can use exactly the same approach to represent something like the actual state of one of the individual qubits, or the closest thing it has to a state. Its state is intrinsically mixed, in reality itself, not just in our minds because we lack information. The mixed description is all the information there is in the world about that one qubit.

We know what that mixed state would look like for the first qubit as a matrix, expressed in the MATHI5a basis, because we already worked out the probabilities:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \frac{3}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix}\]

But this is only obvious because it’s a particularly simple setup. There is a proper way of getting from the density operator of a joint system to the density operator of one of its component subsystems that works even when the answer isn’t obvious. Our combined two-qubit system’s vector space is spanned by the usual basis vectors:

\[\lbrace \, \ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11} \, \rbrace\]

These are shorthands: MATHI5c6b65747b30317d203d205c6b65747b307d205c6f74696d6573205c6b65747b317d and so on. There is a corresponding bra-space:

\[\lbrace \, \bra{00}, \bra{01}, \bra{10}, \bra{11} \, \rbrace\]

These are operators that act on a ket to produce a scalar, the inner product. Or we can write them in reverse as a ket-bra to make all the elementary projection operators (or in matrix form, matrices whose entries are all zero except for a single MATHI31, which can be scaled and added to make any matrix.)

Through the tensor product, the parts of an operation related to one subsystem “find each other” and act independently. We saw exactly this when we applied the Hadamard operator MATHI485e7b5c6f74696d6573206e7d to a whole register of MATHI6e qubits: it’s the same as applying Hadamard to each qubit individually. So these are equivalent:

\[\ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l} = \ket{ij} \bra{kl}\]

So even if we aren’t certain of our joint two-qubit system’s state, and we have to describe it as a density operator rather than a pure state, that’s fine:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l}\]

Here the MATHI69, MATHI6a, MATHI6b and MATHI6c indices range over MATHI5c6c627261636520302c2031205c726272616365, so they are the usual qubit basis state labels. Thus MATHI5c72686f5f7b696a2c6b6c7d symbolises the 16 coefficients of the joint state’s density matrix MATHI5c72686f, each giving a weighting to the tensor product of two single-qubit density operators. MATHI69 and MATHI6a label the kets, while MATHI6b and MATHI6c label the bras.

The exact way we’ve split the indices into different summations carries a significance, even though we could have written them many different ways. Ultimately we need all 16 combinations of the possible index values. But it makes sense to bunch them by which subsystem (qubit) they are driving. To see why, check out the almighty mess we get when we tabulate all the terms of the above sum:

\[\begin{matrix} & k=0, l=0 & k=0, l=1 & k=1, l=0 & k=1, l=1 \\ i=0, j=0 & \rho_{00,00} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{00,01} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} & \rho_{00,10} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{00,11} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} \\ i=0, j=1 & \rho_{01,00} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{01,01} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} & \rho_{01,10} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{01,11} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} \\ i=1, j=0 & \rho_{10,00} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{10,01} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} & \rho_{10,10} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{10,11} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} \\ i=1, j=1 & \rho_{11,00} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{11,01} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} & \rho_{11,10} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{11,11} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} \\ \end{matrix}\]

In each cell we write both the first and second qubit’s ket-bra, stitched together with the tensor product, and also scaled by the coefficient MATHI5c72686f5f7b696a2c6b6c7d that would appear in the density matrix. MATHI69 and MATHI6a drive the rows, whereas MATHI6b and MATHI6c drive the columns.

It’s tricky to spot any pattern to it, but the way we grouped the summation variables doesn’t follow this ket/bra, row/column picture, and this is deliberate:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l}\]

Instead, it divides the labels according to subsystem: MATHI69 and MATHI6b produce the first qubit, MATHI5c6b65747b697d5c6272617b6b7d, whereas MATHI6a and MATHI6c produce the second, MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d5c6272617b6c7d.

The first qubit’s four basis states each relate to one of four quadrants of the table, visited in turn by the MATHI5c73756d5f7b692c6b7d summation. The second qubit lives inside each quadrant as its four entries, visited by MATHI5c73756d5f7b6a2c6c7d. Breaking it down into these quadrants and ignoring the details of the second qubit:

\[\begin{array}{c|c} i=0, k=0 & i=0,k=1 \\ \hline i=1, k=0 & i=1,k=1 \\ \end{array}\]

So there’s a hierarchy to it: the outer structure of quadrants describing the first qubit, the inner entries of each quadrant describing the second qubit. To distil it down to a MATHI32205c74696d65732032 density matrix for the first qubit, we just need “blur our eyes”, turning the details of each quadrant into a single number. This is what the trace does, but here we’re applying it separately to each quadrant, and it’s called the partial trace:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \cdot \operatorname{Tr} \Big( \ket{j}\bra{l} \Big)\]

Recall that MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d, being a basis vector, is a one-hot column. The outer product MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d5c6272617b6c7d in matrix form only ever has MATHI31 in a single entry, the rest being MATHI30, and this single MATHI31 will only sit on the main diagonal if MATHI6a203d206c. This means that the trace is MATHI31 if MATHI6a203d206c and is MATHI30 otherwise, and further means that any term in our summation where MATHI6a205c6e65206c will vanish. This gets rid of half the terms automatically.

Now, if you’re familiar with tensors as they appear in classical physics, you may be wondering why this isn’t just referred to as contraction, and I think you have a point! It is literally just an example of that. QM has its own terminology. Also, the hierarchical arrangement of the two subsystems is completely arbitrary, a byproduct of using matrix notation, and obscures more than it illuminates in my opinion. We don’t have to do it this way.

entry.title: Quantumania 19 - Disappear With Trace
entry.content:
Last time we discovered projection operators, starting with the ket-bra or outer product:

\[\ket{\phi} \bra{\phi}\]

which operates on a vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d by projecting it onto MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d, i.e. scaling MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d by the inner product MATHI5c6272616b65747b5c7068697d7b5c7073697d:

\[\ket{\phi} \braket{\phi}{\psi}\]

It may have occurred to you that such an operator can be thought of as an alternative representation of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d. Rather than representing states as vectors in a vector space, perhaps we could instead represent them with operators acting on that vector space. This is appealing in that it means we represent everything through operators: states, transformations, measurements.

The downside is that it seems a little wasteful when you think about the numerical description of a qubit state in some basis as now requiring four numbers instead of two. But consider also that if we take a representation of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d in some basis as having two coordinates MATHI285c7068695f312c205c7068695f3229, then the outer product produces a matrix:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \phi_1 \\ \phi_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \phi_1^* & \phi_2^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_1 \phi_1^* & \phi_1 \phi_2^* \\ \phi_2 \phi_1^* & \phi_2 \phi_2^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \vert \phi_1 \vert^2 & \phi_1 \phi_2^* \\ \phi_2 \phi_1^* & \vert \phi_2 \vert^2 \end{bmatrix}\]

The diagonal elements are always real, being the modulus squared of some complex number. Furthermore, assuming the basis is aligned with the eigenvectors of some observable, they are the probabilities of obtaining distinguishable measurement outcomes. Also they are all such probabilities, so they must sum to MATHI31.

We’ve talked before about state vectors needing to be unit vectors so that when we interpret their coordinates as complex amplitudes, and take the modulus-squared, we get probabilities. By switching to projection operators as our states, we can replace that requirement by instead saying that the sum of the diagonal entries of the state’s projection operator must be MATHI31. This aspect of a matrix is important enough to have a name, the trace, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d284d29. When we think about matrices we can remember it simply as the sum of the diagonal entries. But perhaps surprisingly, it does not depend at all on our choice of basis. This means we’re not merely talking about the trace of a matrix specific to some numerical representation; we’re talking about the trace of an operator, an invariant basis-independent fact.

To see why, albeit it in a rather laborious way to begin with, recall that to convert a matrix to another orthogonal basis is simply to place it in the sandwich of rotation and un-rotation, MATHI55204d20555e7b2d317d. The rotation takes the form:

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} x & -y^* \\ y & x^* \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{where } \vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 = 1\]

That restriction on the sum of the squares is equivalent (in real vector spaces) to saying:

\[x = \cos \theta \quad \quad \quad y = \sin \theta\]

but we can put that out of our minds. More importantly, the inverse MATHI555e7b2d317d is the adjoint MATHI555e5c646167676572. Let’s make the basis-conversion sandwich around some matrix MATHI4d with any old entries:

\[M = \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix}\]

and multiply it on the left and then on the right:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} M' &=& U M U^\dagger \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} x & -y^* \\ y & x^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x^* & y^* \\ -y & x \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} jx - ly^* & kx - my^* \\ jy + lx^* & ky + mx^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x^* & y^* \\ -y & x \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} jxx^* - lx^*y^* - kxy + myy^* & \dots \\ \dots & jyy^* + lx^*y^* + kxy + mxx^* \end{bmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

I haven’t bothered to write in the off-diagonal entries at the end because we only want the trace, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d284d2729, so we add the main diagonal entries:

\[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Tr}(M') &=& \left( jxx^* - lx^*y^* - kxy + myy^* \right) + \left( jyy^* + lx^*y^* + kxy + mxx^* \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}gather like terms:} &=& \left(jxx^* + jyy^* + mxx^* + myy^* \right) + \left(lx^*y^* - lx^*y^* + kxy - kxy \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}cross terms cancel:} &=& jxx^* + jyy^* + mxx^* + myy^* \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}but $xx^* = \vert x \vert^2$ so:} &=& j\vert x \vert^2 + j\vert y \vert^2 + m\vert x \vert^2 + m\vert y \vert^2 \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}pull out common factors:} &=& j\left( \vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 \right) + m \left(\vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}but $\vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 = 1$ so:} &=& j + m = \operatorname{Tr}(M) \end{align*}\]

The trace is unaffected by the change of basis. It is a fact about the operator described by the matrix, not merely a fact about the specific representation of that operator as a matrix in a particular basis.

Though there’s actually a much simpler way to reach this conclusion. Never mind rotations, consider any three matrices being multiplied together (again we only need the main diagonal entries):

\[\begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} paj + qcj + pbl + qdl & \dots \\ \dots & kar + ksc + mbr + msd \end{bmatrix}\]

Fine. But what do we get if we cycle the three inputs around so the first one moves to third place, second becomes first and third becomes second?

\[\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} paj + pbl + kar + mbr & \dots \\ \dots & qcj + qdl + ksc + msd \end{bmatrix}\]

All the same terms are there, just switched around a bit, but that won’t affect the trace. So for any matrices MATHI412c20422c2043:

\[\operatorname{Tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{Tr}(BCA)\]

This is the cyclic property of the trace. And therefore, as MATHI555e5c6461676765722055203d2049:

\[\operatorname{Tr}(U M U^\dagger) = \operatorname{Tr}(M U^\dagger U) = \operatorname{Tr}(M)\]

So now we’ve got two interesting facts about traces, in addition to the QM rule that for a projection operator MATHI50 representing a state, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d285029203d2031. But we’re still waiting for the states-as-operators idea to really earn its keep by doing something new.

Okay, new scenario. Alice is sending Bob a qubit, and it’s either MATHI5c6b65747b307d or MATHI5c6b65747b317d, and she flips a coin to decide which. So is this a description of the state of the qubit?

\[\ket{+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big)\]

Nope. That’s a qubit state that Alice is definitely not going to send. All the way back at the start we swore never to be wishy washy and always remember that a state is a sharply defined arrow, and if you think of it as a superposition that’s a matter of interpretation. What we have here is sometimes called classical uncertainty. Put more simply, we know Alice is going to send one of two states, we don’t know which one, but we know they’re equally likely.

We can represent this state of knowledge (which is not the same thing as a state as we’ve been using that term so far) by weighting each state projection operator by its probability and adding the results:

\[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0} \bra{0} + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1} \bra{1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]

We can see that this is entirely different from the projection operator for MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d:

\[\ket{+}\bra{+} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

So a matrix can describe our state of knowledge when it has some uncertainty about it, and in this case it’s a different thing from the so-called quantum uncertainty we hear about. There is a fact in the world, and Alice knows that fact, but Bob doesn’t. Alice and Bob would each make a different matrix to describe their own state of knowledge.

Alice would describe her state of knowledge with a pure state, a projection operator that is equivalent to a definite state vector. Bob would describe his state of knowledge with a mixed state (in this context a somewhat misleading term), which is the sum of all the possible pure state matrices, each weighted by its probability. The collective term for these is a density operator, after the classical concept of a probability density function, although it’s more common to hear the matrix representation of such an operator referred to as a density matrix.

But there’s a much more interesting application of these ideas, one which ties together much of the themes we’ve been wrestling with, even the dreaded measurement problem.
